question: According to publicly available sources, in 2026 Germany continues to make substantial payments connected to harm caused during the Second World War, including approximately EUR 924 million in home care for Holocaust survivors worldwide and annual hardship payments of EUR 1 350 per person to over 128 000 recipients.

These payments are negotiated annually between the German Government and the Conference on Jewish Material Claims Against Germany (the Claims Conference). Polish victims of Nazi German aggression, including survivors of mass executions, forced labour and systematic destruction of civilian property, receive no comparable ongoing payments and are excluded from these mechanisms. 1.

Does the Commission consider that the exclusion of Polish victims from these ongoing payment mechanisms, on the basis that they are not covered by the Claims Conference framework, raises issues of equal treatment and non-discrimination under Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU, given that both Jewish and non-Jewish Polish victims suffered?
What could the Commission do to investigate whether this ongoing differential treatment of EU citizens who are victims of the same historical atrocities is compatible with EU fundamental rights law?
answer: EN P-002072/2026 on behalf of the European Commission (26.10.2026) The Commission recalls that the EU rules on state compensation, notably the 2004 Compensation Directive1, apply to applicants whose injuries result from crimes committed after 30 June 2005.

The matter raised by the Honourable Member concerns payments to Holocaust survivors under arrangements negotiated between the German Government and the Conference on Jewish Material Claims Against Germany ‘the Claims Conference’. In light of the above, the situation described falls outside the scope of the EU law.

The Commission further recalls that under Article 51(1) of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU2, its provisions apply to Member States only when they are implementing EU law. Accordingly, the Commission has no legal basis to investigate these payments under EU fundamental rights law unless a concrete link to the implementation of the EU law were established.
1 Council Directive 2004/80/EC of 29 April 2004 relating to compensation to crime victims, OJ L 261, 6.8.2004,
